title: Message ordering
description: Learn about message ordering guarantees in distributed systems. Understand FIFO, causal, and total ordering and when each is needed.

data.text: Message ordering determines the sequence in which messages are delivered to consumers. Different ordering guarantees come with different trade-offs in performance, complexity, and scalability.
Messages may be delivered in any order. This is the default for most distributed messaging systems.

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Independent events, fire-and-forget operations, analytics, when message order doesn't matter for correctness.
First-in-first-out ordering guarantees that messages from the same producer are delivered in the order they were sent.

items: Messages from different producers may interleave

data.title: When to Use
data.text: State updates, commands that must execute in sequence, per-user operations, any scenario where order matters within a stream.
Causal ordering preserves cause-effect relationships. If message A caused message B, then A must be delivered before B.

items: Uses vector clocks or similar mechanisms
Partial ordering—not all messages are comparable

data.title: When to Use
data.text: Collaborative editing, distributed transactions, systems where operations have logical dependencies that must be preserved.
Total ordering guarantees that all messages are delivered in the same order to all consumers. This is the strongest guarantee.

data.title: Use Sparingly
data.text: Total ordering is expensive. Only use it when absolutely necessary. Most systems can work with weaker ordering guarantees.
Different messaging systems provide different ordering guarantees.

items: Kafka: FIFO per partition (partition by key for ordering)
RabbitMQ: FIFO per queue (use separate queues for ordering)
SQS: No ordering (use FIFO queues for ordering)
Pub/Sub: No ordering (use ordering keys in some implementations)

data.text: Design your system to work with the ordering guarantees you can realistically provide.

items: Partition by ordering key—same key goes to same partition
Sequence numbers—let consumers reorder if needed
Idempotency—handle duplicates that may occur with retries
Use application-level ordering when system guarantees aren't enough

data.title: Best Practice
data.text: If you need ordering, partition by the entity that needs ordering (e.g., user ID). This gives you FIFO ordering per user while allowing parallel processing across users.
